#849. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

#848. 'Two faces' & rudely named set-pieces end Hibs' long wait for home win

Marink Reedijk ended Hibernian's long wait for a home league win

Hibernian got an enormous monkey off their back in the battling 2-1 win over Dundee at Easter Road on Tuesday night, finally ending their home hoodoo.

Martin Boyle put them in front from the penalty spot before a glorious Nicky Cadden curler made it two before half-time and those goals proved enough for a first league win in Leith since 4 April.

That is 243 days, or seven-and-a-half months. However you slice it, it's too long for a club of Hibs' stature.

Head coach Marink Reedijk broke that sorry sequence at the fourth time of asking, having lost his previous home games against Falkirk, Celtic and Dundee United.

Before the League Cup semi-final against rivals Hearts at the start of this month, there was talk of the Dutchman being under early pressure.

Instead he secured Hibs' first win over their bitter rivals at Hampden and has now won three of his past four matches.

Are we getting a clearer picture of Reedijk's team and is a corner being turned?

Before the win over a similarly-dejected Dundee, following their 8-0 hammering by Hearts, Reedijk rejected talk of a home jinx.

The notion was a valid one. Hibs had lost nine of their previous 10 home league games, including a 4-0 drubbing by Dundee United at the weekend.

However, the former Beveren manager does not seem prone to superstition or intangibles. He is a straight talker and hammered home the need to nail the "brilliant basics".

Hibs hardly blew Dundee away in front of a sparse Easter Road crowd, but dominated possession and had more accurate passes and balls into the final third than their opponents.

The win was the most important thing and they had to scrap for the three points after Joe Wright hauled Dundee back into the game in the second half.

"It's also capable to show two faces - a nice way of playing football, but also that we can be a team with the knife between the teeth, survive in a match and get over the line," said Reedijk, who is building a reputation for a neat turn of phrase.

On Saturday, Hibs were second to most balls, struggled to show any identity and looked lost tactically.

"I think it's a good reaction to what we did against Dundee United," Reedijk added.

"I saw a front foot team again, I saw togetherness again, I saw a team who fought for every ball.

"That's not easy, they have to be patient, you have to be secure, you have to wait for your moment and we took these moments and that was really good to see.

"As long as we keep ourselves, I think these are good signs."

'An absolute peach!' - watch superb Cadden strike

Cadden's stunning strike came from a smartly-engineered corner routine, with the left-back having gone close from a similar situation earlier in the match.

Reedijk singled out assistant coach Rogier Molhoek for devising the set-piece plans, joking that the codes used are rather rude.

He added: "It was a beautiful goal, wasn't it? It was one when it left the foot, I was like, 'ooh, he hits it well and you saw the angle of the ball'. Then, when I didn't see the keeper getting close to the ball, I was like, 'oh, this is in'.

"We try to use every quality we have in order to make it difficult for opponents to see what we are doing in the beginning. Also we look at their organisation and if their organisation allows us to attack certain spaces, we try to do this.

"This is the job of Rogier, he always makes routines. He will always give a little touch, a little twist, in order to surprise â and also with crazy names. You will never know these names because sometimes it's not polite."

#847. Rangers 'dug it out' despite naivety & complacency - McInnes

Rangers scored three goals in 11 minutes at the start of the second half after a triple substitution

Rangers manager Derek McInnes says his team's naivety and complacency made their task more difficult in their thrilling 3-2 win over Aberdeen, but hailed their ability to get the job done.

The Ibrox outfit had to navigate a tense finale as they held off a defiant Aberdeen side, just three days after their dramatic late win at Motherwell, and are now just a point behind Celtic at the Scottish Premiership summit.

Rangers had roared into a 3-1 lead after a stunning 11-minute burst at the start of the second half overwhelmed the visitors, who led at the break through Brad Lyons' header.

However, the Dons pulled one back through vibrant youngster Findlay Marshall and both sides had opportunities to add to the scoreline in a gripping closing passage.

"We put ourselves in the mire there, we were so naive at times," McInnes told Sky Sports.

"The biggest part for me is how we lose the initiative by just being too complacent and that has to change because we won't always outscore opponents.

"Once we got ourselves in front you think 'just keep the shoulder to the wheel'. We hit them like a train and they were 3-1 down because of the speed, intensity, intelligence and then we started to play backwards.

"We played more backwards passes than I can remember in a long time, we need to show more control."

Rangers beat Aberdeen in five-goal thriller to move within one of Celtic

McInnes' displeasure at the first-half display manifested itself in a half-time triple substitution as Findlay Curtis, Tuur Rommens and Kim Min-Su were hurled into the action.

Rangers were a different team in the 11 minutes that followed, with goals from Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin turning the game on its head and flipping the mood of the Ibrox faithful.

"For us it was all about winning, we've won the game and we'll dust ourselves down," McInnes added after a 14th straight game without defeat.

"It was three good goals and I'm delighted by the impact of the subs and we dug it out, but we made it harder for ourselves."

That ability to grind out wins was evident at Fir Park on Saturday and was apparent again at Ibrox. Belief is growing among Rangers supporters, who are longing for a first league title in six years.

They have won six points from losing positions this season, a tally bettered only by St Johnstone and Celtic, who have seven apiece.

A win over Falkirk on Saturday, before Celtic travel to face Hearts on Sunday, would put Rangers top of the table for just the second time this season.

For the umpteenth time this season, Rangers were indebted to in-form striker Naderi.

The 23-year-old struggled for a consistent run of games in the early stages of his Ibrox career, but has more shown his worth with Youssef Chermiti and Lawrence Shankland sidelined through injury.

He has 13 goal contributions in 13 league appearances - eight goals and five assists - and also fired Rangers into the Premier Sports Cup final with his winner against Aberdeen at Hampden earlier this month.

"A lot of players have had plaudits recently, but where would Rangers be without Naderi?," former Rangers striker Kris Boyd asked on Sky Sports.

"He's scored big goals for Rangers this season. His goal return has been outstanding and they're big, big goals for Rangers."

Naderi, who featured twice for the Czech Republic during the international break, has the Scottish Premiership's highest expected goals (xG) and xG per 90 minutes.

His perfectly weighted assist for Gassama showed the touch of a player full of confidence and playing at the peak of his powers.

After weathering an early Rangers storm, Aberdeen took the lead and looked well worth their advantage at half-time.

For all of their endeavour and late surge, they failed to recover from their 11-minute capitulation. Still, Aberdeen legend Willie Miller was heartened by the performance under new head coach Mario Frick.

"It's been a long time since I've seen a performance as good as that from an Aberdeen side, albeit it was a defeat," Miller said.

"They pushed Rangers all the way. It will be a learning process for them, you'd certainly hope that would be the case."

15-year-old Andrew Fasanya's introduction shows Frick has no issues playing young players who merit game time, and 20-year-old Marshall was perhaps the standout performer of the night.

"When Aberdeen got their second, they gave as good as they got," McCall added.

"It's the type of game, and Aberdeen will be gutted to have lost it, but you can see progress, an idea, a bond with the supporters.

"A young Scottish player [Marshall], I thought was the best player on the park, too."

Andoni Iraola's Liverpool revolution continues, as another big-name transfer shapes up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool and Bayern Munich might be about to shake hands on an intriguing transfer move in which big names move on either side.

The last two summers have been two of the biggest transfer windows in Liverpool's history, with three £100 million players joining the club in a recruitment revolution, following the end of the Jurgen Klopp era.

And things might be about to get even more extraordinary, with Bayern Munich “increasingly likely” to sell one of their biggest names – and the Reds front and centre for his signature.

Despite critics pointing to a lack of balance in their forward options over the summer, Liverpool are starting to find rhythm in attack under new manager Andoni Iraola, as the likes of Bradley Barcola, Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Rio Ngumoha all performed well in the weekend's 4-1 victory over Manchester United.

With Wirtz and Ngumoha both targets of Bayern Munich, however, the balance may be about to shift again – with the Bavarians now “increasingly likely” to sell Jamal Musiala.

Musiala has struggled this season with what he has described as “neurological dysfunction” this season, with honourary Bayern president Uli Hoeness has faced significant criticism for comments in which he questioned whether Musiala will ever return to his best form for Die Roten, stating, “What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what was stipulated in the contract” he signed at the Allianz Arena.

TEAMtalk reports that Liverpool and Arsenal are now interested in Musiala, with Bayern now potentially open to selling a previously untouchable asset – paving the way for either Wirtz or Ngumoha to leave.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that the latter is in talks over a new contract, but with Wirtz having struggled in English football since briefly becoming the Reds' all-time record transfer, he may welcome a return to the Bundesliga, where he made a name for himself as one of the biggest talents in world football and won the title with an invincible Bayer Leverkusen side.

It has recently been suggested in the German media that Wirtz and Musiala aren't naturally compatible in the same team, with journalist Christian Falk likening the pair's jostling for a place as Die Mannschaft's No.10 as similar to the battle between Gunter Netzer and Wolfgang Overath for a place in West Germany's 1974 World Cup side.

Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard, meanwhile, has been linked with a move to Bayern – while the Gunners could field Musiala on the left wing.

Transfermarkt values Musiala at €80m. Liverpool face Club Brugge tonight in Champions League action.

#845. Murrell flourishing at high-flying Falkirk after 'random' move

Jacob Murrell has hit the ground running with Falkirk since his move from the United States

"It was completely random," is how Jacob Murrell describes his summer switch from DC United to Falkirk.

Now the 22 year-old American is the joint-leading scorer in the Scottish Premiership, with eight goals from 11 starts.

His tremendous form has helped Falkirk surge up the table, with six successive victories taking them from 11th to third place.

"I was looking for more minutes as a young player and Falkirk kind of came out of nowhere," he explained. "They called my agent and a week later I was in Scotland.

"It happened really fast and it was a crazy path to get here. I was just desperate to play. I wasn't happy just being a training player.

"I wanted to win games and score goals and now both are happening."

A Maryland native, the 6ft, 3in centre forward played college football at Georgetown on his way to being a super draft pick for DC United in 2024.

A big Baltimore Ravens fan, Murrell is settling into his new surroundings, although he is wary of the cuisine, telling BBC Scotland he has no plans to try haggis or black pudding.

"The first month was difficult but the club supported me the whole time, making sure I was sound and pushing me to follow my dream.

"Team-mates, staff and fans have all been so good to me and made me feel at home in such a short period of time.

"I grew up north of Baltimore and I'd been in that hour-and-a-half DC radius my entire life with my friends and family, so leaving was really hard.

"Stepping out of my comfort zone has taught me a lot about myself, having to adapt and grow up."

Murrell, the league's player of the month for October, was one of 17 summer signings made by John McGlynn, who ended the club's 15-year absence from the top flight via back-to-back promotions.

"The manager has been so good for me, instilling confidence from day one," he said. "He backs me to score goals and be an influential part of the team."

A first visit to Ibrox is next up for Murrell as Falkirk take on second-placed Rangers on Saturday.

"I'm just taking it day by day, my next focus is Rangers and trying to make it seven on the bounce," he adds.

"Things can turn fast so we need to remember where we came from, stay humble and keep working hard."

#844. Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.

Aston Villa star Alejandro Garnacho is looking increasingly bereft in the Midlands following comments from manager Unai Emery.

After three wins in their opening three Champions League fixtures, Aston Villa have now lost their last two, with a 1-0 defeat to Galatasaray following the loss against Barcelona – and with Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund on the horizon, the Europa League winners face an increasingly tough ask to finish within the league phase's top eight and avoid a play-off place.

It doesn't look hopeful for Garnacho to be involved in either match, following Emery's post-match comments in Istanbul.

TEAMtalk have described the Basque boss's 19-word statement on Garnacho's absence as “humiliating”, when asked about why the winger was excluded from the squad to face Gala.

Garnacho was once labelled as an exciting talent at Manchester United, but was shipped out to Chelsea at the start of last season in a move that would net the Red Devils pure profit on his sale, and failed to light up Stamford Bridge last season – before joining Villa on loan over the summer.

Despite this, the 22-year-old has played just seven times under Emery, all off the bench, with the Villa boss saying after the game, “Today the players who were here are who I think are the best players to be here with us.”

Garnacho will make his move permanent if he makes a certain number of appearances for the Villans this season, as he looks to replace Morgan Rogers, who left Villa Park for a club-record nine-figure fee over the summer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But rather like Liverpool's Harvey Elliott last term, the winger hasn't impressed Emery in his limited showings, having clocked up 96 forgettable minutes thus far in claret-and-blue.

Elliott played just four times in the Premier League under Emery after it became clear that the five-time Europa League-winning coach didn't see a place in his team for the England under-21 star.

Emery later described the loan move as “embarrassing for everyone involved”, publicly apologising to the player for a move that he believed stunted his development as a midfielder.

FourFourTwo understands that Villa are already looking to back out of a permanent transfer for Garnacho, who moved to Villa along with Nicolas Jackson from the Blues.

These deals are just two of a plethora between the two clubs in recent years, including Jadon Sancho, Axel Disasi, Ian Maatsen, Emiliano Martinez, Carney Chukwuemeka and Omari Kellyman, with both sides criticised for exploiting the Premier League's Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR).

Transfermarkt values Garnacho at €22m. Villa play Ipswich Town away this weekend, as Premier League action continues.

#842. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, he comes up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posts them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#841. Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A pregnant person with dengue speaks to a nurse in Peru, which has been hit by a surge of cases this year. Credit: Juan Carlos Cisneros/AFP/Getty

The debilitating viral disease called dengue has exploded in incidence far more than previously thought, a new analysis suggests.

The number of reported global cases of dengue, which is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, rose from 430,000 in 1990 to 14.7 million in 2024 — a 34-fold increase, the analysis says.

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

The data were presented on 22 November at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH) in National Harbor, Maryland. Scientists also provided some of the strongest results yet about a counter-intuitive way to curb the disease’s staggering spread: the release of specially modified mosquitoes. But researchers also presented discouraging data on other solutions, and scientists at the meeting emphasized that the campaign to beat back dengue will be complicated and costly.

“We’re in an extraordinary and pivotal moment” in the history of studying mosquito-borne illnesses, said Albert Ko, president of ASTMH. Trial results presented at the meeting showed, he said, that “we can get rigorous evidence on what works, what doesn’t and what needs to be done to scale these effective interventions to protect the 4 billion people” around the world who are exposed to dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses.

Dengue causes fever, headaches and severe bone pain. It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, a species of mosquito that thrives in warm, urban environments. Global warming and increased urbanization have expanded the mosquitoes’ range. Existing vaccines provide imperfect protection.

Cases of dengue are often recorded in disparate databases that aren’t easily comparable, says Ahyoung Lim, an infectious-disease modeler at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who was involved in the study on dengue incidence. The results have also been published as a preprint1 on Research Square ahead of peer review. This has meant that no single database has captured the total number of reported dengue cases over time, leading Lim and her team to compile the most complete record of reported cases and use statistical modelling tools to fill in gaps in which data were missing.

The staggering increase in reported cases isn’t surprising, says Eng Eong Ooi, a dengue virologist at Duke–NUS Medical School in Singapore who was not involved in the research. Populations in urban environments around the world are steadily increasing, he says, which means that “more and more people are living at risk of dengue each year”.

One promising approach to curb dengue starts with breeding mosquitoes and deliberately infecting them with a bacterium called Wolbachia that reduces the insects’ ability to transmit viruses. When released into the wild, these infected mosquitoes pass the bacterium on to their offspring, eventually lowering the number of highly transmissive mosquitoes.

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

At the ASTMH meeting, another team of researchers shared results from the first randomized controlled trial in the Americas to test Wolbachia’s effect on dengue transmission. Between January 2021 and May 2022, the researchers released roughly 32 million Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes across designated regions of Brazil and monitored almost 6,000 children living inside and outside these regions. The children provided annual blood samples between 2020 and 2024, and the reseachers found that those in the Wolbachia regions were 68% less likely to be infected with dengue compared with those in non-Wolbachia regions.

These positive results mark an important milestone in proving Wolbachia’s potential to drastically reduce dengue cases, says Elisabeth Nelson, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health in New Haven, Connecticut, and a researcher on the trial.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03813-6

#840. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Newcastle United's owners PIF are seeking fresh investment to help the club achieve its infrastructure goals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.

Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.

However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.

First and foremost, PIF are not packing their bags and walking away from St James’ Park.

Rather than offloading existing shares to pocket a profit, the club is issuing brand-new equity - with US investment bank J.P. Morgan appointed to find an external partner.

This means not a single penny from the sale will flow back into PIF’s coffers - they are not recouping on their investment. Instead, funds raised through the share issue will supposedly be injected into Newcastle's ongoing projects.

PIF will see its majority stake diluted rather than exiting the club, remaining firmly in the driving seat as owners with majority control.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While fans have grown increasingly frustrated by delays around major infrastructure upgrades, the club, led on the executive side by chief executive David Hopkinson, remains engaged in long-term plans to either substantially redevelop St James’ Park or build a brand-new stadium altogether, alongside the construction of a state-of-the-art training complex.

Bringing in additional investment allows Newcastle to raise hundreds of millions in fresh equity to accelerate those builds, sharing the heavy financial lifting.

After a difficult summer that saw stars like Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon depart to help balance the books, developing Newcastle’s infrastructure and off-pitch revenue streams is the only sustainable way to compete with Europe's elite.

Since original consortium member Amanda Staveley sold her shares and left the board in 2024, ownership of the Magpies has been split between just two parties: PIF holds an 84 per cent majority stake, while the London-based Reuben family - represented on the board by Jamie Reuben, via RB Sports & Media - owns the remaining 16 per cent.

Issuing new shares to cover a 25 per cent stake will dilute both PIF and potentially the Reubens proportionally, leaving PIF with comfortably over 60 per cent of the club and still overall control.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#838. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

#837. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

#835. Sinner to miss Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery

Jannik Sinner won the Australian Open in 2024 and 2025 but will miss the 2027 edition due to knee surgery; Tennis Australia confirmed his absence from the opening Grand Slam of the year; Sinner has not played since winning Wimbledon in July

Jannik Sinner will miss the Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery, tournament organisers have announced.

The world No 2 has not played since defending his Wimbledon title in July, seeing Alexander Zverev overtake him at the top of the world rankings.

Sinner confirmed on Tuesday he had undergone minor surgery on his right knee, extending his injury lay-off and leaving his participation in the first Grand Slam tournament of 2027 - starting January 17 - in doubt.

The Australian Open hinted at his likely absence by posting on social media that they would miss Sinner this summer, with Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo confirming that Sinner will not take part in Melbourne.

"We've been in regular touch with Jannik's team and they've confirmed he won't be joining us for the Australian Open in January following his recent surgery," Abdo said.

"Jannik loves competing here in Melbourne and is looking forward to returning for the Australian Open in 2028."

Sinner said earlier this month he was confident of returning in time for the Australian Open but would not rush recovery, with the 25-year-old since confirming the surgery on his knee was due to experiencing ongoing pain .

Sinner said in a statement earlier this week: "Over the past few months, together with my team, we've tried everything to treat my injury without surgery.

"After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn't respond as we had all hoped, that's why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band.

"I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team."

The iliotibial band is a thick band of fibrous connective tissue running down the outside of the thigh, and injuries associated with it are typically caused by overuse.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sinner had made a stellar start to 2026 which saw him win the first five Masters 1000 tournaments of the year, becoming the second man after Novak Djokovic to achieve the Golden Masters.

Zverev and world No 3 Carlos Alcaraz supported Sinner's decision to undergo surgery, with his Grand Slam title rivals looking forward to being able to welcome him back to the court.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"The decision of making the surgery, I think his team made a good decision," Alcaraz, the defending Australian Open champion, said on Wednesday.

"He's young, has a lot of years ahead of him. I'm sure he's going to come back even stronger, even better."

Sinner won his first Grand Slam singles title in 2024 by beating Daniil Medvedev in five sets at Melbourne Park, then defended it by winning the 2025 final against Zverev.

Zverev added: "We know that he's mentally strong. I hope that he takes every step serious and that, in three, four months' time, he can be back to 100 per cent and be back playing."

#833. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

#832. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

#831. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Yeremy Pino is the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow-card suspension

Crystal Palace's Yeremy Pino has become the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow card suspension after accumulating five bookings since the 2026-27 season began.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash were the first players to receive a ban for collecting five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 17 players sitting on four bookings after 11 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have received a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (five yellow cards)

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Chema Andres - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Yeremy Pino - Crytsal Palce (yellow card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

Costinha - Brighton & Hove Albion (red card suspension)

Leny Yoro - Manchester United (red card suspension)

James Tarkowski - Everton (red card suspension)

#829. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

#827. Why Man City can't wear their new kit in Premier League

Manchester City will only be wearing their orange kit for selected Champions League games

Manchester City sported a new orange fourth kit during their Champions League draw with Napoli on Tuesday - but will not be able to wear it in the Premier League.

Top-flight clubs in England can only wear a maximum of three strips in a league campaign, meaning Enzo Maresca's side cannot play in their new kit.

However, there is no limit in the Champions League, meaning City can wear their new strip for the rest of their European campaign.

City can also wear the kit in the FA Cup, provided that an application is made to the Football Association, as well as a reason for its requested use.

That is why Arsenal were allowed to play in a white fourth strip in the 2025-26 FA Cup as part of their campaign to combat youth knife crime in London.

Fans could scan the badge on City's 2025-26 fourth kit to receive items in a video game

City also released a green fourth kit in 2025-26 with a gaming-inspired theme.

The kit, debuted during their Champions League victory over Villarreal, featured an NFC chip in the club badge that fans could scan to unlock gaming rewards.

The club released another fourth kit in the 2024-25 season co-designed by Noel Gallagher in tribute to the 30th anniversary of Oasis' 1994 album 'Definitely Maybe'.

It was worn in the Champions League by the men's team against Inter Milan and Paris St-Germain, and the women's team against Paris FC and Barcelona.

A fifth kit was also used by the men's team during the 2025 Club World Cup

During the 2023-24 season, the women's side also sported a Chinese New Year-inspired shirt in a League Cup victory against rivals Manchester United.

While the Premier League is more restrictive over the number of kits that can be released - the rules are more relaxed in other European leagues.

Napoli wore 13 strips during the 2021-22 season; including a Halloween kit, four different Diego Maradona tributes and four Europa League-specific kits.

#826. Watford have appointed another new manager - not even Pep Guardiola would be a success at Vicarage Road

The more things change, the more they stay the same - Watford is an unmanageable club

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has gone turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

However, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

After Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or plan - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

Bradley is a sports journalist and Watford fan, who previously spent seven years working for talkSPORT. During his time with the station, he covered the Premier League, EFL and WSL, as well as the Lionesses, and interviewed the likes of Pep Guardiola, Ange Postecoglou, Mikel Arteta, Sarina Wiegman, Alessia Russo, Hannah Hampton and Oscar among others. In his spare time, he is the commentator for Non League side Harefield United. Previously, he worked for Newsquest, covering both Watford and Leyton Orient for the Watford Observer and East London Guardian Series newspapers. He has also had pieces published in the Daily Mail and Watford's matchday programme.
